title: Mandaadi: A Thrilling Sailboat Drama with Mixed Reviews
excerpt: Critics find it engaging but uneven, with strong performances and thrilling visuals.
body:
• Soori delivers a career-best dramatic turn as Muthukaali, a disgraced champion sailboat racer seeking redemption — critics are near-unanimous on this.
  • The sailboat racing sequences, shot on open water by S.R. Kathir, are the film's towering achievement and unlike anything in recent Tamil cinema.
  • The screenplay follows the sports-drama rulebook closely, and a stretched flashback in the second half stalls the momentum.
  • Critical consensus: 3.0–3.5 stars across major publications — a flawed but rousing entertainer carried by its performances and its sea.

There is a moment just before the interval in Mandaadi when Muthukaali, played by Soori, stands alone against Sattapuli's men — and then against Sattapuli himself, played by Suhas — in a fight involving heavy swords and a literal harpoon. It is a pure mass moment, staged with total conviction, and it announces something the Tamil film industry has been slow to accept: Soori, the comedian-turned-hero, can carry an action film on his shoulders. That sequence, and the film around it, is why Mandaadi has become one of the most discussed Tamil releases of the season.

Directed by Mathimaran Pugazhendhi, Mandaadi is built around a sport most viewers have never seen: traditional sailboat racing off the Ramanathapuram coast. Muthukaali (Soori) was once a champion racer and the protégé of Matchamuni (Sathyaraj). A tragedy twenty years ago — revealed in a flashback that arrives deep in the second half — drove him into exile in Chennai, where he now works as a lifeguard at an amusement park, a wryly chosen profession for a man running from the sea.

He is pulled back when Maari (Mithun Jai Shankar), a young hothead fleeing Sattapuli's wrath, seeks him out. Sattapuli (Suhas) — once Muthukaali's closest friend, now his bitterest enemy — runs the dominant Tsunami Riders team and a fibre-boat business built on his father's name. Maari wants to raise a team of local boys to beat him. Muthukaali sees his shot at redemption and agrees to coach them.

What the Critics Say

Sreeju Sudhakaran, Rediff.com (3.5/5): The most enthusiastic of the major critics, Sudhakaran argues the film "makes the rulebook look quite good." He singles out the interval fight and the race sequences, noting the mechanics of sailboat racing are "simplified for audiences who do not understand how these races work, without ever baby-talking to them." He calls the practice match "a clear standout sequence" and praises the climax race — complete with a literal whirlpool and a mid-sea fight — as overboard in the best way. On performances, he writes that Soori delivers "easily one of the finest lead performances in Tamil cinema this year," and calls Suhas "brilliant as the antagonist," elevating a role the writing doesn't fully support. His chief complaint: the flashback "not only stalls the pacing right at the start of the second half, but is also where the commonplace nature of the plot hits its most ordinary, predictable low."

Roopa Radhakrishnan, The Times of India (3.0/5): Radhakrishnan finds Mandaadi "an uneven ride but it has enough going for it." She credits the final race sequence — "teased throughout the film" — with elevating the otherwise uneven narrative, and praises G.V. Prakash Kumar's score as "rousing without being overly loud." She notes Soori brings "a groundedness" to Kaali that another actor might have made erratic, and that Suhas turns a potentially one-note villain into "a menacing" presence. Her structural critique centers on the delayed flashback: "since the flashback comes much later in the narrative, we aren't able to fully feel the weight of those reactions." She also flags small textured details — "a peace meeting being held in a dargah" — that give the village specificity, and notes the film's conscious effort to give its women purpose rather than sidelining them.

Akshy Kumar, Cinema Express (3/5): Kumar's review, headlined "Scintillating sail despite some turbulence," praises how the watersport was captured as "breathtaking" and finds the unfamiliarity of the sport itself refreshing — the rules, the sabotage, the genuine danger of injury and death all deliver "cinematic highs." But he cautions the writers sometimes got "carried away and over-excited, like the audience, thereby dramatising some of these sequences a tad excessively." He takes issue with the film's commercialization subplot — drawing IPL parallels for a sport unique to Ramanathapuram district feels "a stretch." On Soori: "looks exceptional as Muthukaali," with an emotional arc he calls brilliant, though some late-film stunts strain believability. He reserves special praise for the film's cultural documentation — the tsunami's aftermath, the shift to diesel fibre boats, and the argument for preserving traditional sailing.

Yashaswini Sri, The Indian Express (3/5): "Soori, Suhas are extraordinary on water, the film drifts when on land," Sri writes, capturing the critical consensus in a headline. She credits Soori's physical performance with burnishing "his growing reputation as a serious leading man" while finding the screenplay unable to sustain its unique premise across the full runtime.

Bhuvanesh Chandar, The Hindu: Chandar locates the film's strength in "layered characters and assured performances from Soori and Suhas," reading it as a socio-political sports actioner rather than a pure genre exercise.

The Scenes That Matter

Three sequences define the film. The interval fight — Muthukaali against Sattapuli's men, escalating to a harpoon duel with Sattapuli himself — is the film's mass-movie thesis statement. The practice match, where the underdog local team first shows its mettle, is the sequence critics cite most as pure cinema. And the climax race, with its whirlpool and mid-sea combat, divides critics on execution (the VFX is uneven) but unites them on impact.

Quieter moments land too: the scene where Soori's Muthukaali apologizes to Angel (Mahima Nambiar) is singled out by Sudhakaran as hitting "all the right emotions," and Nambiar's fierce confrontation scenes in the second half showcase an actress refusing to be background in a male-bravado showdown.

The Verdict

Mandaadi doesn't reinvent the sports drama — every critic agrees the underdog-vs-powerhouse template, the redemption arc, and the delayed flashback are familiar. What it does is execute that template around a genuinely unfamiliar sport, with a lead performance of real gravity and race sequences shot on actual open water. The flashback placement is the film's most-cited flaw; the sea is its most-cited triumph. At roughly 140 minutes, it's a substantial, rousing watch — and further proof that Soori's transformation from comic sidekick to leading man is the real thing.

The Videshi rating: 3.25/5 — consensus of 6 major critics. In theaters now; streaming date to be announced.
